to flip Live Updates

Ballot issues are reported in some areas with pivotal elections that will decide control of Congress.

Video Ad Feedback Watch CNN's coverage of midterm elections • Source: CNN Watch CNN's coverage of midterm elections Ad Feedback Election Day in America • Trump lashes out: As Americans head to the polls, President Donald Trump fumed over coverage of his election eve remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool yesterday, writing on social media that reporters misinterpreted his jokes about renaming the pool in his honor.

• At the polls: Minor voting issues have been reported in some areas, with voting machines in the key swing district that includes Westchester County, New York, unable to scan ballots, and flooding in Florida forcing 23 polling locations to move. Voting is currently underway across the US, and the first polls are due to close at 6 p.m. ET.

• High stakes: Democrats, who need a net gain of three seats to capture the House and four seats in the Senate, enter Election Day with a 9-point advantage in the generic congressional ballot, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls. The GOP’s redistricting strategy will be put to the test, and the party is defending Senate seats in firmly red states.

• Election monitors: The Justice Department says around 1,000 election monitors have been deployed in 126 jurisdictions in all 50 states — many of which are Democratic strongholds.

• Stay with us: Follow CNN’s tracker of when to expect results and sign up for breaking news email alerts to get key updates.

Trump says the country is watching New York on Election Day By Alejandra Jaramillo President Donald Trump listens to a reporter's question in the Oval Office of the White House on September 28. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images President Donald Trump has a message for New York voters on Election Day: The whole country is watching.

“TODAY, the eyes of the Country are on New York again!” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post, as he repeated his endorsement of Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, who is defending his seat in one of the country’s most competitive House races.

Lawler’s district covers Rockland County and part of Westchester County, where polling sites have had issues with voting machines today.

New York Attorney General Letitia James said her office is monitoring the issue and is in touch with state and local election boards. “Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will count,” she wrote on X.

The president praised Lawler as “a tremendous friend to the Jewish community and a strong leader in the fight against antisemitism.”

Link Copied! Trump to host White House viewing party after allies wanted to watch results with him By Kristen Holmes at the White House President Donald Trump will watch the midterm results come in with a small group of allies and Cabinet members in the East Room tonight, while the White House and Trump’s political operation, MAGA, Inc, have war rooms set up on campus and nearby to monitor the results, sources said.

One source said the viewing party came together in recent days, as Republican officials and allies told the White House that they hoped to watch the results with the president.

The scene will be reminiscent of how Trump watched the 2022 results. And while the circumstances could hardly be more different for Trump than they were in 2022, the outcome could be similar.

Back then, Trump, having finished his first term and departed Washington, was planning a political comeback, one that he believed would be boosted by candidates he endorsed posting massive wins.

In the final stretch of the race, Trump put himself on the ballot as he campaigned with his chosen candidates. On election night, he held a watch party at Mar-a-Lago and invited the press to watch what he and his advisers at the time believed could be a Republican landslide.

But as the night went on, it became clear that those candidates that had embraced the MAGA agenda flamed out in some of the most high-profile races. The press was quickly ushered out as Trump fumed at his staff over their role in helping choose the candidates.

Tonight, Trump will once again gather with top aides and advisers to watch the midterm results, this time as president of the United States, having completed the political comeback he sought. Yet, the White House is bracing for similar, potentially disappointing results.

Sources close to Trump said he has, at times, seemed hopeful that the polling was wrong, and that his party will be more successful than they suggest. Trump has told aides that he thinks his involvement — including campaign spending, telerallies, and trips to fundraise and promote Republican candidates — gave Republicans a fighting chance.

However, he has also privately conceded that his party may be facing the worst case scenario, the sources said. Two White House officials said that they would be ready for any scenario, including Trump choosing to speak to reporters as the results were coming in.

Link Copied! Cabinet members stay optimistic as they prepare for results at the White House By Kevin Liptak Members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet have been filing through the West Wing today as aides and advisers prepare to absorb tonight’s results.

They have adopted an optimistic air as the voting unfolds across the country.

“Today is a big day,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said after a television interview on the White House lawn.

“I don’t know that there will ever be a time in history that is marked with more success than what President Trump has led these last couple of years,” Rollins said before heading into the West Wing.

A few hours later, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said he was “super optimistic about the future of the country and where it’s going,” and predicted positive economic news in the coming years.

He said he would spend the evening at the White House, where Trump is hosting a results watch party in the East Room.

Cabinet officials have been campaigning heavily over the past month for Republicans, looking to tout the administration’s accomplishments.

Burgum joined Trump Monday at his speech from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where the president mostly discussed his renovation projects around Washington.

Many Republicans were left scratching their heads at the choice of venue for Trump’s final speech before Election Day. But Burgum insisted it made perfect sense.

“It’s a perfect spot to basically say to America that just like closing the border was a choice, just like cutting taxes was a choice, just like cutting regulations was a choice, Americans do not have to accept decline and squalor in our major cities,” he said.

“You can choose to have a beautiful and clean city,” he went on. “Any mayor and any governor could do what President Trump did here in Washington, DC. It’s a role model for the country.”

Link Copied! Top House Democrats confident in taking control of the House tonight By Manu Raju Top House Democrats are bullish that they will take the House of Representatives tonight and that they will have a more comfortable majority than the razor-thin one that Speaker Mike Johnson currently holds.

Publicly and privately, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries doesn’t want to get too far ahead, saying that he thinks they will get at least 218 seats, which is a majority. But two top Democratic sources tell CNN that they think they can win between 230 to 235 seats. A huge tsunami would mean as many as 240 seats, but Democrats view that as less likely than around 230 to 235 seats.

Jeffries has been more cautious. According to a person familiar with the matter, Jeffries started the day in New York and traveled to Washington, DC, where he had lunch with party officials. But the crab shack they lunched at was the same place Democrats dined at during Election Day 2018 — the last time Democrats flipped the House under President Donald Trump, when they picked up 41 seats.

Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc./Getty Images Election results will start rolling in in a matter of hours. So how to keep track of the battle for the House?

A good way is to read this piece outlining which House races will determine whether Democrats win the majority, have a blue wave, or even see something larger like a tsunami.

Link Copied! What is likely to happen if Democrats win control of Congress Analysis by Zachary B. Wolf If Democrats can win control of the House, the Senate or both, they will change the power dynamic in Washington for the end of President Donald Trump’s second term in office.

There are some areas where this power will be most obvious.

Oversight — Democrats would have powerful new tools to investigate Trump’s government.

Spending — They would have a seat at the table when it comes to how taxpayer dollars are spent and also potentially a mandate to undo some of the changes Trump has imposed.

Priorities — Democrats could also pass partisan bills as a show of their priorities on topics like the Iran war, tariffs, immigration and elections.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who would be House speaker if Democrats win control, has cited three immediate goals:

► Ending the war to bring down energy prices.

► Undoing cuts to Medicaid in the Republican tax and spending cuts bill, and renewing Obamacare’s enhanced premium subsidies to address health care costs.

► Repealing Trump’s tariffs to bring down the costs of goods.

Expect vetoes. There are limits to what the Democratic caucus would be able to accomplish. And maintaining unity and resolve would take work, especially since Trump might not be willing to work with them to keep the government functioning. The threat of funding lapses — more commonly known as government shutdowns — could be a recurring theme.

“What happens is I veto everything, and then the Democrats come and they want to make a deal,” Trump said last week of the prospect of working with a Democratic-majority Congress.

It takes 67 votes to overturn a veto in the Senate, a higher bar than the 60 votes it takes to pass meaningful legislation.

There could also be opportunities for bipartisan progress. During Trump’s first term, after Republicans lost control of the House, he worked with Democrats to pass the First Step Act, a key piece of sentencing reform legislation.

Link Copied! Johnson set to watch results in Louisiana, with future as speaker hanging in the balance By Annie Grayer in Shreveport, Louisiana House Speaker Mike Johnson speaks during a campaign event in Linglestown, Pennsylvania, on October 28. Joe Lamberti/Getty Images House Speaker Mike Johnson returns to his home district in Louisiana for election night, hoping that his extensive travel schedule, massive fundraising haul and close allegiance with President Donald Trump will be enough to save his job.

But most Republicans say the results on Tuesday will determine Johnson’s future.

Johnson is expected to huddle with top aides and advisors, watching results in real time and calling candidates, according to a source familiar with Johnson’s plans. He is expected to be in a war room at some point Tuesday night, but it depends on the weather, the source added.

Johnson’s homecoming to Shreveport, Louisiana, comes after a month-long campaign sprint on the road with 91 candidates and GOP members across 24 states and 45 districts, the source told CNN. Raising an eye-popping $156 million this cycle, his team says Johnson has raised the most of a speaker or leader to date.

In the final weeks of the campaign, Johnson has been adamant that the polls reflecting a difficult political environment for Republicans are wrong, and that he will remain Speaker of the House. Multiple sources describe Johnson as a “happy warrior” both publicly and privately.

Johnson has not entertained a world where Republicans do not hold onto the majority, and so he has not indicated what he plans to do if Republicans lose the House, according to a source in Johnson’s orbit.

But Johnson allies say that Republicans should not count the Speaker out.

“He’s always been underestimated. Everyone has made assumptions about him and he’s always risen to the challenge,” the source said.

If Democrats flip the House by a massive margin, multiple Republican lawmakers and sources told CNN they expect House Majority Leader Steve Scalise and House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan to start making calls as early as Tuesday night, since Republican leadership elections are just a week away.

Both Scalise and Jordan have said they support Johnson and are trying to help Republicans hold the majority. But the two men have been laying the groundwork for a possible run, the GOP lawmakers and sources told CNN.

CNN has reached out to both teams for comment.

“If we keep the majority, Johnson will run unopposed,” one Republican lawmaker, who has campaigned with Johnson, told CNN. “If there is a wave, he will not be there, and I hope he would recognize that, and I think he would, and step aside because that would really be a pretty bitter fight within the party.”

Another Republican told CNN that Johnson doesn’t get to decide his own political future, the results will.

“If we lose by a little bit, he can make the argument, ‘well it could have been a lot worse because of how hard I worked.’ If we lose by a lot, I think it becomes more challenging,” the GOP lawmaker said.

Voter and self-identified Republican Ronald Turner told CNN's Danny Freeman he had doubts about voting for Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick but voted for him because "he's a Republican" at a polling place in purple Bucks County, Pennsylvania.

Pennsylvania voter bothered by gas prices, but still supports Trump and Iran war 1:39 At a polling place in purple Bucks County, Pennsylvania, voter and self-described Republican Ronald Turner told CNN the Iran war was the “the best thing (President Trump) could have done.”

“I don’t like paying higher prices, but if it’s going to keep me from getting blown up down the road, I more than welcome it,” Turner said today.

Turner said he thinks Trump is doing great in his second term and voted for Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick — who is in a competitive race in Pennsylvania’s 1st Congressional District — even though he feels Fitzpatrick could support the president more.

“I had my doubts about Fitzpatrick, but I went with him anyway (because) he’s a Republican,” Turner said.

Link Copied! DHS focuses its messaging on voter fraud on Election Day By Michael Williams The Department of Homeland Security is publicizing the arrests of noncitizens accused of voting or registering to vote in past elections as voters head to the polls today — while warning that federal law enforcement will track down and arrest anyone who votes illegally in this year’s midterms.

Voter fraud, including voting by noncitizens, is exceedingly rare, although the Trump administration and DHS have claimed that it is rampant.

“If you vote illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you,” Immigration and Customs Enforcement said on X. “There will be no escape.”

For weeks leading up to this year’s election, DHS has promoted the arrests of noncitizens accused of registering to vote or voting in previous elections.

Although top officials had initially claimed that tens of thousands of noncitizens voted in past elections, those numbers have fallen apart under scrutiny.

CNN’s Priscilla Alvarez contributed to this report.

Link Copied! Poll workers at Mount Kisco in Westchester await guidance on transporting ballots By MariaSole Campinoti and Gloria Pazmino, in Mount Kisco, New York Poll workers at a voting location in Mount Kisco, New York, have been processing voters and their ballots all day, but they are still awaiting instructions about what to do once polls close at 9 p.m. ET.

Voters are placing their paper ballots in orange emergency ballot bags, with one bag designated for each election district in the village of Mount Kisco, CNN observed Tuesday.

Mount Kisco has seven election districts, meaning poll workers expect all paper ballots to be collected in seven separate orange emergency ballot bags. Once all ballots are collected, the bags will be brought to the Village of Mount Kisco Manager’s Office, according to a local election poll worker who asked not to be identified.
